rationale: Start with a broad, moderately steep gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Increase temperature while keeping the gradient fixed to probe selectivity of the sole under-resolved pair. The other pairs have resolution headroom, and the last peak is already comfortably within 10 minutes.

The central peak pattern suggests a temperature-driven elution-order crossing between 40 and 50 C; moving to 55 C may separate that pair further. A gentler gradient should help protect the neighboring pair that tightened at 50 C, while targeting a last peak within 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is already achieved, so shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to measure the effect on the marginal central pair.

Shorten the gradient another step to test the fastest fully resolved method at 55 C. The central pair improved at 14 minutes, but the neighboring pair at R = 1.77 may now become limiting; retain injection 4 as the fully resolved fallback.

Lower the starting organic fraction to test whether altered early-gradient selectivity restores the newly limiting pair while retaining the shorter gradient. Injection 4 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test a cooler selectivity regime with a shorter gradient to seek another fully resolved window. The 55 C methods are constrained by two neighboring pairs, so a larger temperature shift may offer more room to accelerate the separation.

Explore a hotter, steeper gradient for a substantially faster separation and a possible alternative elution-order window. This tests whether temperature-driven selectivity can compensate for gradient compression; injection 6 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Raise the starting organic fraction to probe whether the under-resolved pair separates further in the apparent reversed-order window at 60 C. This also targets a shorter elution time, while monitoring the neighboring pair currently at R = 2.00.

Test whether a steeper gradient improves the reversed-order critical pair at 60 C without compressing its neighbor below baseline resolution. Returning to phi0 = 0.10 protects the early pair that became under-resolved at phi0 = 0.20.

Test the cooler side of the promising 40 C separation, where the central pair may move away from its apparent temperature-driven crossing. Keeping the original gradient isolates temperature selectivity and should keep the last peak within 10 minutes.

Probe whether a steeper gradient at 40 C opens a faster selectivity window for the central cluster. The lower starting organic fraction should preserve early-peak retention; injection 6 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved fallback.

Test an intermediate temperature in the fast-gradient regime, seeking a better balance between the central pair and its neighbors than at 40 or 60 C. The low starting organic fraction preserves early retention while targeting an elution window near six minutes.

Shorten the fastest confirmed fully resolved method by one gradient step, holding its endpoints and temperature fixed. This directly tests the speed boundary near injection 6, with particular attention to its two marginal pairs.

Use an intermediate gradient slope between injections 4 and 5 by lowering the final organic fraction one step. This targets recovery of the limiting pair to R ≥ 1.5 with an elution time close to the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction and steeper gradient improve the central pair at 50 C, where its neighboring pair had more resolution headroom than at 55 C. This explores a potentially faster fully resolved window while avoiding the early-peak compression seen at phi0 = 0.20.

Lower the final organic fraction one more step from injection 15 to lift its R = 1.47 pair above baseline resolution. This should retain a last peak below 10 minutes and may provide more balanced resolution margins than the fastest confirmed method.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step from injection 4 to test whether reduced initial retention can shorten a fully resolved separation. Monitor the central cluster closely, since changing the starting composition also changes selectivity and gradient slope.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction can separate the limiting central pair at 50 C while a gentler slope protects its neighbors. The cooler temperature may also preserve the early pair that was compressed at this starting composition at 60 C.

Refine between injections 15 and 17 with a gradient slope of 0.065 organic fraction per minute, targeting full resolution with a last peak around 7.8 minutes. This should improve the limiting pair relative to injection 15 while shortening the separation relative to injection 17.

Test a slope of 0.080 between the fastest fully resolved method’s 0.075 and injection 14’s under-resolved 0.090. This targets a modest speed improvement while directly bracketing the limiting pair’s resolution boundary.

Preserve injection 6’s successful gradient slope while ending the programmed ramp sooner at a lower organic fraction. The gradient should remain unchanged through the observed 7.60-minute elution window, targeting the same maximum CRF with a shorter ramp and lower final organic content.

Raise temperature one grid step from injection 22 to test whether its maximum-score separation can be accelerated. Monitor the central pairs for selectivity loss; retain injection 22 as the fully resolved fallback.

Return to 55 C and preserve the successful 0.075 gradient slope through the critical cluster, but begin the final hold earlier. This tests whether a shorter programmed gradient and lower final organic fraction retain full resolution and elution within 10 minutes.

Test a final hold beginning near the central cluster to see whether reduced gradient compression improves the limiting pair at 50 C. The maximum CRF is already secured; injection 22 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method with the shorter programmed ramp.
